title: Finetuning: 500m AI agents in production with 2 engineers — Mustafa Ali & Kyle Corbitt

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's core subject is fine-tuning an 8B LLaMA 3.1 model via distillation from o3-mini to meet production quality, cost, and latency targets that off-the-shelf models could not satisfy simultaneously. The application is financial liability data extraction for fintechs, banks, and lenders, and the workflow is an internal enterprise data-processing pipeline scaled to production. The discussion centers on moving an existing GPT-4 agentic workflow from initial production deployment through large-scale productionization at 16M requests/day. Requires familiarity with agentic workflows, fine-tuning, distillation, and API cost structures, but is presented as an accessible engineering case study. Two practitioners present a detailed real-world case study of their production deployment journey and fine-tuning solution. All key claims are directly stated in the transcript with quantitative backing from the speakers.

summary: Method Financial collects and centralizes liability data from hundreds of sources to serve fintechs, banks, and lenders. When customers demanded specific data points like auto loan payoff amounts and mortgage escrow balances, no central API existed. Direct bank integrations would take years, and the status quo involved offshore contractor teams calling banks manually—an expensive, slow, error-prone process. Method built a GPT-4 agentic workflow to parse unstructured data, which worked well but cost $70,000 in the first month. Prompt engineering hit a wall since GPT-4 isn't a financial expert, requiring long instructions with constant fixes. Scaling targets were 16 million requests/day, 100K concurrent load, and sub-200ms latency. OpenPipe partnered with Method to address quality, cost, and latency. They benchmarked GPT-4 (~11% error rate) and o3-mini (~4% error rate) using human-verified ground truth. Neither model met all requirements: GPT-4 failed on error rate and cost, while o3-mini failed on latency (~5s) and cost due to reasoning tokens. Method's post-processing plausibility checks meant they didn't need 0% error—around 9% was acceptable. OpenPipe then fine-tuned an 8-billion-parameter LLaMA 3.1 model using distillation, generating training outputs with o3-mini from existing production data. The fine-tuned model achieved better-than-GPT-4 accuracy, far lower latency, and dramatically lower cost, exceeding Method's viability thresholds. The smaller model could even be collocated with application code to eliminate network latency. Key enablers included already having production data from GPT-4 usage, using the cheapest sufficient model, and not needing to buy GPUs. Productionizing AI agents requires patience from engineering and leadership, as unlike traditional code, AI systems take time to reach production readiness.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introductions and Company Backgrounds
sections.summary: Kyle Corbitt (OpenPipe) and Mustafa Ali (Method Financial) introduce themselves. Method Financial collects and centralizes liability data from hundreds of sources and serves enhanced data to fintechs, banks, and lenders for debt management. OpenPipe helps build, train, and deploy open source models using production signals for continuous improvement.

sections.title: The Problem: No Central API for Liability-Specific Data
sections.summary: Customers wanted liability-specific data points like payoff amounts and escrow balances, but no central API existed. Direct bank integrations would take years. The status quo involved offshore contractor teams calling banks manually—an expensive, slow, synchronous, error-prone process. Method recognized the core problem was parsing unstructured data, which LLMs like GPT-4 could potentially solve.

sections.title: GPT-4 Solution and Scaling Challenges
sections.summary: Method built a GPT-4 agentic workflow that worked well for extraction tasks but cost $70,000 in the first month. Prompt engineering hit a wall as GPT-4 isn't a financial expert, requiring long convoluted prompts with constant cat-and-mouse fixes and no versioning. Caching couldn't be optimized, latency was slow, and hallucinations were hard to catch. Method's scaling targets: 16M requests/day, 100K concurrent, sub-200ms latency.

sections.title: OpenPipe Partnership and Performance Measurement
sections.summary: OpenPipe began working with Method to address quality, cost, and latency. They measured error rates (GPT-4 ~11%, o3-mini ~4%) using human ground truth, latency (GPT-4o ~1s, o3-mini ~5s), and cost (o3-mini more expensive despite lower per-token cost due to reasoning tokens). OpenPipe emphasized measuring under real production conditions with diverse tasks and production-level concurrency.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning Solution and Results
sections.summary: Neither GPT-4 nor o3-mini met all three requirements simultaneously. Method's post-processing plausibility checks meant ~9% error rate was acceptable. OpenPipe fine-tuned an 8-billion-parameter LLaMA 3.1 model using distillation—generating training outputs with o3-mini from existing production data. The fine-tuned model achieved better-than-GPT-4 accuracy, far lower latency, and dramatically lower cost, exceeding Method's viability thresholds. The smaller model could be collocated with application code to eliminate network latency. Key enablers: existing production data from GPT-4, cheapest sufficient model, no GPUs needed. Only two engineers were needed. Productionizing AI agents requires patience from engineering and leadership, as unlike traditional code, AI takes time to reach production readiness.
